canonical_statement: The study objective was to characterize internists' dosing practices when administering and adjusting intravenous heparin regimens.
The investigators administered a physician-led survey to 61 attending internists at two community teaching hospitals and one Veterans Affairs Medical Center.

population.label: Attending physicians in internal medicine surveyed at three teaching hospitals

canonical_statement: Survey questions were framed around a hypothetical 70-kg patient with confirmed deep venous thrombosis; no age, gender, or comorbidity information was supplied.

population.label: Hypothetical 70-kg patient with confirmed deep venous thrombosis

canonical_statement: All three hospitals used plain Dade Actin thromboplastin reagent on automated MLA systems, with an approximately 20-30 second normal APTT control range.
The survey assumed that each APTT measurement was obtained at least six hours after any change in heparin dose.
The survey elicited initial bolus and infusion doses, therapeutic APTT range, and bolus/hold/infusion responses across APTT bands <1.2, 1.2-1.5, 1.5-2.3, 2.3-3.0, and >3.0 times control.
Surveyed physicians had a mean age of 40.6 years (range 30-65); 69% were general internists, 31% subspecialists, 68% community-based, and 32% full-time hospital teaching faculty.

population.label: Attending physicians in internal medicine surveyed at three teaching hospitals

canonical_statement: When a respondent gave a numeric range for a requested discrete value, the investigators used the midpoint of that range for calculations.
Proportions were compared with chi-square analysis; continuous variables were analyzed with two-tailed Student t tests, with paired t tests used for within-group mean comparisons.
The mean initial heparin bolus was 6,925 units (SD 2,427), with a 1,000-12,000 unit range and a 5,000-unit mode.

canonical_statement: The mean initial heparin infusion was 1,029 units/hour (SD 141), with a 500-1,500 units/hour range and a 1,000 units/hour mode.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that intravenous heparin dosing practices varied widely among internists at the three hospitals and that dosing choices varied coherently with physicians’ chosen APTT therapeutic goals.

The authors argued that variation in APTT reagent responsiveness is a major obstacle to standardizing therapeutic APTT ranges and limits transportability of nomograms across laboratories using different test systems.

The authors stated that scientific consensus about the optimal initial intravenous heparin dose was still evolving and that empirical guidance for subsequent dose-adjustment decisions was even more limited.
The study surveyed physicians’ reported practices rather than auditing their actual heparin dosing behavior.
The investigators, rather than the physicians, selected the APTT intervals used as decision nodes in the survey.

The study defined control APTT as the upper limit of the laboratory normal range, an approach the authors noted was not universally accepted; five respondents instead used the patient’s pretreatment APTT as control.
The 61 surveyed physicians did not include all clinicians using intravenous heparin at the three hospitals, so selection bias was possible.

Attending physicians at teaching hospitals may not represent all internists who prescribe heparin, particularly because detailed heparin dose management may be performed by house staff in such settings.
The authors called for experimental studies comparing standardized intravenous heparin dosing protocols before physician education or standardized practice guidelines could be expected to succeed.
